Predicting Concrete Compressive Strength¶

A regression case study: can we predict how strong a concrete mix will be from its recipe and age?

Executive summary¶

A tuned neural network predicts concrete compressive strength to within about 2.9 MPa on average (MAE), with RMSE 4.6 MPa and R² 0.93 on 201 held-out samples (mean strength is about 35 MPa). Gradient boosting performs essentially the same (RMSE 4.5 MPa), and both are far more accurate than linear regression (RMSE 7.4 MPa).

  • Biggest driver: curing age, followed by binder (cement) content and water.
  • What moved accuracy most: sound evaluation design and domain-informed features (log of age, water/binder ratio), more than model complexity. These features alone lifted linear regression from R² 0.59 to 0.82.
  • Honest expectation for new recipes: when whole recipes are held out of training, error rises to roughly 5 MPa RMSE (R² about 0.89 to 0.90), because the dataset repeats each recipe at several ages.

1. Business context and question¶

Concrete strength is measured by crushing test cylinders after curing (commonly 28 days), which is slow and costly. If strength can be predicted from the mix recipe and age, engineers can screen candidate mixes before casting them, cut lab testing, and spot mixes that are likely to under-perform.

Question: how accurately can compressive strength (MPa) be predicted from the ingredients (kg per m³ of concrete) and age (days), and which factors drive it most?

Data: the public UCI Concrete Compressive Strength dataset (Yeh, 1998), 1,030 laboratory samples.

Column Meaning Unit
cement, slag, flyash Binder materials kg/m³
water, superplasticizer Water and chemical additive kg/m³
coarseaggregate, fineaggregate Gravel and sand kg/m³
age Curing time at testing days
csMPa Target: compressive strength MPa

Method in brief: audit the data, explore it, build a leakage-free evaluation (split first, preprocess inside a pipeline), compare simple baselines against a neural network, tune the network, test once on held-out data, then check how well results hold up on mixes the model has never seen.

# Remove exact duplicates BEFORE splitting, so a repeated row cannot land in both train and test.
df = raw.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)

Rows after removing duplicates: 1,005 (dropped 25)

Audit findings: no missing values, all columns numeric, and a small number of exact duplicate rows, which were removed. The ranges look physically plausible (for example, water of roughly 120-250 kg/m³, strength of roughly 2-83 MPa), so no values were treated as errors.

What the exploration shows

  • Strength is mildly right-skewed, and the age relationship is strongly curved, so a straight line in raw age will under-fit. Log of age should linearise much of it.
  • Cement and superplasticizer are positively related to strength; water is negatively related.
  • Some inputs are correlated with each other (for example, water with superplasticizer), which matters when interpreting importance later.

Feature engineering from domain knowledge. In concrete engineering the ratio of water to cementitious material is a primary driver of strength (lower is stronger). I add four row-wise features: water_cement, binder (cement + slag + fly ash), water_binder, and log_age. They are computed row by row with no fitted statistics, so creating them before the split does not leak information.

In [6]:
def add_features(frame):
    out = frame.copy()
    out["water_cement"] = out["water"] / out["cement"]
    out["binder"] = out["cement"] + out["slag"] + out["flyash"]
    out["water_binder"] = out["water"] / out["binder"]
    out["log_age"] = np.log(out["age"])
    return out

TARGET = "csMPa"
RAW_FEATURES = [c for c in df.columns if c != TARGET]
ENG_FEATURES = RAW_FEATURES + ["water_cement", "binder", "water_binder", "log_age"]

data = add_features(df)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
sns.scatterplot(data=data, x="water_binder", y=TARGET, hue="log_age", palette="viridis",
                alpha=0.6, ax=axes[0], legend=False)
axes[0].set(title="Lower water/binder ratio means higher strength",
            xlabel="Water / binder ratio", ylabel="Compressive strength (MPa)")
sns.scatterplot(data=data, x="log_age", y=TARGET, alpha=0.45, ax=axes[1], color="#3b6ea5")
axes[1].set(title="Log of age straightens the curve", xlabel="log(age in days)", ylabel="Compressive strength (MPa)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

5. Evaluation design¶

Choices that make the results trustworthy:

  1. Split first. 80% of rows for training and model selection, 20% held out and used once at the end.
  2. No leakage. Scaling is fitted inside a Pipeline, so it only ever sees training data (fitting a scaler on all rows before splitting lets information from the test set leak into training).
  3. Cross-validation on the training set (5 folds) for model comparison, instead of judging models on a single split.
  4. Metrics in units people understand: RMSE and MAE in MPa, plus R².
  5. Baselines first. A neural network is only worth its complexity if it beats simple models.
In [7]:
X_all, y_all = data[ENG_FEATURES], data[TARGET]
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_all, y_all, test_size=0.2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
print(f"Train: {len(X_train)} rows   Test (held out): {len(X_test)} rows")

CV = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
SCORING = {"r2": "r2", "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error", "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error"}


def mlp(hidden=(36, 6), alpha=1e-4):
    # The target is standardised too, which helps the network converge on a 2-83 MPa range.
    return TransformedTargetRegressor(
        regressor=Pipeline([
            ("scale", StandardScaler()),
            ("mlp", MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=hidden, alpha=alpha, max_iter=3000,
                                 early_stopping=True, n_iter_no_change=20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)),
        ]),
        transformer=StandardScaler(),
    )


MODELS = {
    "Mean baseline": lambda: DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"),
    "Linear regression": lambda: Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("lr", LinearRegression())]),
    "Random forest": lambda: RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1),
    "Gradient boosting": lambda: GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3,
                                                           subsample=0.8, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Neural network (36, 6)": lambda: mlp((36, 6)),
}


def cv_summary(model, X, y, cv=CV, groups=None):
    res = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, groups=groups, scoring=SCORING, n_jobs=-1)
    return {"R2": res["test_r2"].mean(), "R2 sd": res["test_r2"].std(),
            "RMSE": -res["test_rmse"].mean(), "MAE": -res["test_mae"].mean()}

Train: 804 rows   Test (held out): 201 rows

6. Model comparison (cross-validation on the training set)¶

Every model is run on two feature sets: the 8 original columns and the 12 engineered columns.

In [8]:
rows = []
for feature_name, cols in [("Original 8", RAW_FEATURES), ("Engineered 12", ENG_FEATURES)]:
    for model_name, make in MODELS.items():
        s = cv_summary(make(), X_train[cols], y_train)
        rows.append({"Model": model_name, "Features": feature_name, **s})

cv_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("RMSE").reset_index(drop=True)
cv_table.round(3)

Reading the comparison

  • Every model beats the mean baseline (RMSE 16.0 MPa) by a wide margin.
  • Engineered features help every model, most of all linear regression: R² rises from 0.59 to 0.82 and RMSE falls from 10.2 to 6.8 MPa, because log of age and the water/binder ratio capture curved relationships that a straight line cannot.
  • Tree ensembles lead on cross-validated RMSE (gradient boosting 4.5 MPa). The untuned neural network is behind them at about 5.4 to 5.6 MPa, which the tuning in the next section is meant to close.

7. Tuning the neural network¶

A small grid over network size and L2 regularisation (alpha), scored by 5-fold cross-validation on the training set only. The grid includes the smaller (36, 6) architecture used in the comparison above as a reference.

In [10]:
param_grid = {
    "regressor__mlp__hidden_layer_sizes": [(36, 6), (64, 32), (128, 64), (64, 32, 16)],
    "regressor__mlp__alpha": [1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1],
}
search = GridSearchCV(mlp(), param_grid, cv=CV, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1, refit=True)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

best_params = {k.replace("regressor__mlp__", ""): v for k, v in search.best_params_.items()}
print("Best network settings:", best_params)
print(f"Cross-validated RMSE: {-search.best_score_:.2f} MPa")

tuning = (pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_)[["param_regressor__mlp__hidden_layer_sizes",
                                             "param_regressor__mlp__alpha", "mean_test_score"]]
          .rename(columns={"param_regressor__mlp__hidden_layer_sizes": "hidden layers",
                           "param_regressor__mlp__alpha": "alpha", "mean_test_score": "cv_rmse"}))
tuning["cv_rmse"] = -tuning["cv_rmse"]
tuning.sort_values("cv_rmse").head(6).round({"cv_rmse": 3}).reset_index(drop=True)

8. Final evaluation on the held-out test set¶

The test set has not been used for any decision so far. Three candidates are refitted on the full training set and scored once: the interpretable baseline, the best tree ensemble, and the tuned neural network.

In [11]:
final_models = {
    "Linear regression (engineered)": MODELS["Linear regression"](),
    "Gradient boosting (engineered)": MODELS["Gradient boosting"](),
    "Neural network (tuned)": search.best_estimator_,
}
test_rows, preds = [], {}
for name, model in final_models.items():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    p = model.predict(X_test)
    preds[name] = p
    test_rows.append({"Model": name,
                      "RMSE (MPa)": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, p)),
                      "MAE (MPa)": mean_absolute_error(y_test, p),
                      "R2": r2_score(y_test, p)})
test_table = pd.DataFrame(test_rows).sort_values("RMSE (MPa)").reset_index(drop=True)
test_table.round(3)

Reading the test results

  • The tuned neural network reaches RMSE 4.6 MPa, MAE 2.9 MPa and R² 0.93 on 201 held-out samples. That is essentially tied with gradient boosting (RMSE 4.5, MAE 3.1) and about 38% lower RMSE than linear regression (7.4). Gradient boosting is slightly ahead on RMSE and the neural network on MAE, a gap too small to trust on a 201-sample test set, so I do not claim a winner between them.
  • Error is modest across curing ages (MAE roughly 2 to 3.5 MPa) and highest for 8 to 28 days, where most samples sit.
  • Error grows with strength: MAE is 1.8 MPa for weak mixes (under 20 MPa) but 6.2 MPa above 60 MPa, where training data is thin (18 test samples) and the model tends to under-predict the strongest mixes.
  • Two samples are missed by more than 25 MPa. They have an outsized effect on RMSE (4.6) relative to MAE (2.9) and would be the first rows to check for measurement error or unusual mixes.

9. Does it hold up on mixes the model has never seen?¶

This dataset contains the same recipe tested at several ages. A random split can put one age of a recipe in training and another in testing, which makes scores look better than they would be on a genuinely new mix.

To check, I rebuild cross-validation so every recipe (the seven ingredient columns together) is kept entirely in one fold, using GroupKFold, and compare it with ordinary shuffled cross-validation on the same data.

In [14]:
ingredients = [c for c in RAW_FEATURES if c != "age"]
groups = pd.factorize(data[ingredients].round(2).astype(str).agg("|".join, axis=1))[0]
print(f"{len(data):,} samples from {len(set(groups)):,} distinct recipes "
      f"({len(data) / len(set(groups)):.1f} ages per recipe on average)")

robust_rows = []
for name, make in [("Linear regression (engineered)", MODELS["Linear regression"]),
                   ("Gradient boosting (engineered)", MODELS["Gradient boosting"]),
                   ("Neural network (tuned)", lambda: mlp(best_params["hidden_layer_sizes"], best_params["alpha"]))]:
    random_cv = cv_summary(make(), X_all, y_all, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))
    group_cv = cv_summary(make(), X_all, y_all, cv=GroupKFold(n_splits=5), groups=groups)
    robust_rows.append({"Model": name,
                        "RMSE random folds": random_cv["RMSE"], "RMSE new-recipe folds": group_cv["RMSE"],
                        "R2 random folds": random_cv["R2"], "R2 new-recipe folds": group_cv["R2"]})
robust = pd.DataFrame(robust_rows)
robust["RMSE increase (MPa)"] = robust["RMSE new-recipe folds"] - robust["RMSE random folds"]
robust.round(3)

1,005 samples from 427 distinct recipes (2.4 ages per recipe on average)

Model RMSE random folds RMSE new-recipe folds R2 random folds R2 new-recipe folds RMSE increase (MPa)
0 Linear regression (engineered) 6.924 7.046 0.818 0.810 0.122
1 Gradient boosting (engineered) 4.209 4.986 0.932 0.905 0.777
2 Neural network (tuned) 4.588 5.288 0.919 0.892 0.700

Reading the result

The 1,005 samples come from 427 distinct recipes (about 2.4 ages each). When whole recipes are held out, error rises for the flexible models: gradient boosting goes from 4.2 to 5.0 MPa RMSE (R² 0.93 to about 0.90) and the neural network from 4.6 to 5.3 MPa (R² 0.92 to 0.89). Linear regression barely changes (6.9 to 7.0 MPa) because it cannot memorise recipes, but it is far less accurate overall.

Practical takeaway: for genuinely new mixes, expect roughly 5 MPa RMSE, not the 4.2 to 4.6 MPa that random splits suggest. Both flexible models still beat linear regression by about 2 MPa on unseen recipes.

10. What drives strength?¶

Permutation importance on the held-out test set: shuffle one feature at a time and measure how much the error grows. A bigger increase means the model relies on that feature more.

In [15]:
final_nn = final_models["Neural network (tuned)"]
imp = permutation_importance(final_nn, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=30, random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
                             scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1)
imp_df = (pd.DataFrame({"feature": X_test.columns, "increase": imp.importances_mean, "sd": imp.importances_std})
          .sort_values("increase"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.barh(imp_df["feature"], imp_df["increase"], xerr=imp_df["sd"], color="#3b6ea5", ecolor="grey")
ax.set(xlabel="Increase in RMSE when the feature is shuffled (MPa)",
       title="Feature importance (tuned neural network, test set)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
imp_df.sort_values("increase", ascending=False).round(3).reset_index(drop=True)

Reading the chart

Curing age (as log_age) is by far the most influential input: shuffling it raises RMSE by about 12 MPa. Binder content, cement and water come next, in line with concrete science (more cementitious material and less water mean higher strength). Raw age scores low only because log_age carries the same information. The same logic applies to the ratios and the ingredients they are built from, so read importance by group rather than feature by feature.

11. Limitations and next steps¶

  • Small, historical lab dataset (about 1,000 samples). Results describe these mixes and test conditions, and should not be assumed to hold for other cements, admixtures or curing practices.
  • Repeated recipes make random-split scores optimistic, as section 9 quantifies; the new-recipe numbers are the honest expectation for unseen mixes.
  • Correlated features (the engineered ratios overlap with their parts) share importance, so individual importance scores should be read as a group, not as exact effects.
  • Tuning was modest. The best alpha (0.1) sits at the edge of the search grid, so a wider search could improve the network slightly, and the tree models were left at reasonable defaults.
  • No uncertainty estimate per prediction. For real screening decisions, prediction intervals (for example from quantile gradient boosting or conformal prediction) would be the next addition.
  • Next steps: tune the tree ensemble with the same rigour as the network; add prediction intervals; test on newer or external concrete data; wrap the model in a small web app where a user enters a recipe and age.

Conclusion¶

  • Answer to the question: concrete strength can be predicted from recipe and age to within about 3 MPa on average (MAE) and 4.6 MPa RMSE (R² 0.93) on held-out samples. For genuinely new recipes, plan for roughly 5 MPa RMSE.
  • Model choice: the tuned neural network and gradient boosting perform about equally, and both are much better than linear regression (RMSE 4.6 vs 7.4 MPa). As a default I would start with gradient boosting, which is quicker to train and easier to explain, and keep the neural network as a close alternative.
  • What mattered most: evaluation design (split first, pipelines, cross-validation) and domain-informed features moved results more than model complexity.
  • How it could be used: screening candidate mixes before casting them, for example flagging mixes whose predicted strength falls within a few MPa of the target, until per-prediction uncertainty intervals are added.

Reproducibility¶

Fixed random seed (42), all preprocessing inside pipelines, a single held-out evaluation, and no private data. Requires pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib and seaborn, all preinstalled in Google Colab. Data: Yeh, I-C. (1998), Modeling of strength of high-performance concrete using artificial neural networks, Cement and Concrete Research 28(12); UCI Machine Learning Repository.
